From the Greek philos (love) and sophia (wisdom). Wisdom here means discernment (vivek), not memory. It is called the mother of all disciplines because every field began as a question humans asked when life troubled them.
The Indian word, from the root drish: to see. A philosopher sees something about the world and life that ordinary looking does not show.
The eye of wisdom. The same eyes now see something deeper, because thinking has moved beyond fixed categories such as yes/no and good/bad.
Opening poem: to be for or against any ideology, your stomach must first be full. Philosophy needs a full stomach and free time, which humans did not have for most of their history.
The most popular branch: what is the world ultimately, what is it made of, and where does its diversity come from. Its three deepest questions concern creation, God and the soul.

nodes.l: Cosmology: how did the world form?
nodes.d: Creationism says God made it; evolutionism says it developed on its own; a middle view says God set a basic structure and evolution did the rest. The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old and life about 3.7 billion.
Some traditions believe in God; Jainism and Buddhism do not; Taoism and Confucianism hold God differently. Believers then ask what God is like and what He does.

About 70,000 to 75,000 years ago, Homo sapiens' larger brain, its prefrontal cortex and language allowed complex thought, shared rules, morals and the state. Brain size alone is not the answer: an elephant's brain is larger.
About 10,000 years ago humans learned farming, no longer had to wander or kill for every meal, and gained surplus and leisure. Systematic thinking, philosophy and science grew from this.
Regarded as the West's first philosopher, in the 6th century BC, only about 2,800 years ago. The speaker warns against claims that philosophy is millions of years old.
Parmenides, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Aristotle and Herodotus belong to the same era, when a few Greek cities had the leisure and conditions to think.

Niyativada versus Sankalpa Swatantrya: do we really choose our actions? Determinism is the stronger argument, yet society cannot punish, reward or function without assuming free will, so we proceed as if it is real.
German pessimist who said the luckiest are those never born. The speaker contrasts him with Indian thought, which names suffering but ends in liberation.
The study of how we know. If you claim something is true, philosophy asks for your Pramana: perception, inference, or testimony.
The Vedas and Upanishads. Most ideas Hindus hold today (soul, Moksha, rebirth) were already settled by the Upanishads.
A reaction to heavy ritual and animal sacrifice. Charvaka, Jainism and Buddhism arise.
The Vedas are reinstated as proof. Short memory-friendly sutras give us the six Astika schools.
Around the time Islam arrived, scholars wrote Bhashyas on the Vedanta sutras. Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva, the Bhakti saints and Sikhism belong here.
19th and 20th century India's own renaissance and reform, giving Neo-Vedanta. The speaker compares it with Europe's Renaissance and Reformation.
The speaker adds a sixth phase: Ambedkar, Krishnamurti and Osho, with Iqbal just before independence.
After the Vedas and Upanishads, books recognise nine schools: three Nastika (Charvaka, Jain, Buddhist) and six Astika.
In this classification it is not about God or the afterlife. Astika means accepting the Vedas as proof; Nastika means not taking them as proof just because they are written.

Charvaka, Lokayata and the Brihaspati tradition are one school. It is a group rather than one person and is called Dehatmavada: the living body is the soul, and there is no separate soul. Consciousness arises from matter, as intoxication arises from ingredients like betel and liquor. It denies rebirth and karma; its answer to suffering is: come in the evening and enjoy. The speaker adds that quantum physics is nearing what Charvaka said.
Charvaka is believed to have developed from the philosophy of Sage Brihaspati. The names Charvaka, Lokayata and Brihaspati point to the same tradition.

A materialist teacher of the Charvaka or Lokayata line, named for his hair blanket. The lecture calls him the first Indian voice to say plainly that there is no soul, heaven, hell, rebirth or karma, and compares him with Leucippus and Democritus. The early texts give him four elements, which dissolve at death.
The view that the body is the soul: a living body has a soul only while alive, and nothing separate survives.
The modern echo of Charvaka's claim: mind emerges from physical neurons working together.
Does not believe in God. Mahavira is the 24th Tirthankara.

The 24th Tirthankara, living in roughly the same region and era as the Buddha (present-day Bihar). By the speaker's arithmetic he died at Pava about a year after the Buddha's enlightenment; the Buddha's own last meal was in the same town 44 years later. Makkhali Gosala walked with him for six years before parting. There is no record that the two met.
A profound Jain view of knowledge and the limits of statements. The speaker says it is a deep basis of what we now call Artificial Intelligence.
Rejects the Vedas as proof and a permanent soul, but accepts rebirth and Moksha.

Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda. Mostly mantras for ritual and worship; little philosophy in the early parts. Some give them 10,000 years; the generally accepted view dates their composition to about 1500 BCE, give or take two or three centuries.
Samhita (mantras), Brahmana (procedures), Aranyaka (conduct of forest dwellers) and Upanishad.
The last part of the Vedas, hence 'Vedanta': pure philosophy. Soul, Moksha and rebirth are fixed here.
Mimamsa's claim: the Vedas were not composed even by God; they are eternal and uncreated.
Those who accept the Vedas as Pramana. Six of them make the Shad Darshan, called Hindu or Sanatana philosophy.
The six: Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa and Vedanta, working in joint pairs.
Formulas that state a profound idea very briefly so it can be remembered before writing was common. They are hard to understand without commentary.
Paired with Yoga. Its sutra is attributed to Sage Kapila, though the original text has not been found.
Close companion of Samkhya in one group.
Paired with Vaisheshika; its Sutra is by Akshapada Gautama.
Works jointly with Nyaya, each accepting what the other develops.
Treats the Vedas as uncreated; its idea of Moksha is lighter than Vedanta's.
The dominant school. The speaker says 90 to 95 per cent of what Hindus believe is Vedanta. Its sources are the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutra.
Author of the Samkhya Sutra.
Wrote the Nyaya Sutra (not the same Gautama as the Buddha).
Author of the Brahma Sutra; some identify him with Ved Vyasa.
Teaches Vedanta and is the text most Hindus identify with. It states the immortal soul most clearly.
Because sutras are cryptic, scholars explained them. Interpreting Vedanta meant commenting on the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutra.
From South India, died at 32 after building a profound philosophy. Said only Brahman is ultimately real.
Only Brahman is the absolute truth. God, we and the world are true only at the practical level, like a video game you can step out of.
The world and even God are true on the vyavaharika (practical) level; only Brahman is true in the end.
Mahayana philosopher who explained Avyakrita through Madhyamaka Shunyavada. His ideas resemble Shankara's so closely that some call Shankara a 'disguised Buddhist'.
Devotees of Vishnu who challenged Shankara by putting devotion at the centre.
The first to take Shankara head-on, with Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism).
Active around Agra, Mathura and Vrindavan; Ballabhgarh is named after him. Surdas was his devotee.
Gave Dvaitadvaita.
From Karnataka and Shankara's fiercest critic; his philosophy is Dvaita (dualism).
Great devotee of Krishna; his school is Achintya Bhedabheda (inconceivable difference and non-difference).
The shared purpose of the Vaishnava Acharyas: to establish the tradition of devotion.
In Ramanuja's line; his student was Kabir Das.
Bhakti saint; many of his verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Bhakti poet in Ramanuja's tradition.
Founder of Sikhism, whose approach is close to Kabir's.
A philosophical development of the medieval period; it also holds rebirth.
Vedanta reshaped in the 19th century to present Hinduism as one, answer Western charges of division, and tie philosophy to nationalism and equality.
The scholar who coined 'Neo-Vedanta', sarcastically, since it made converting Hindus harder.
Started the Brahmo Samaj, combining Hindu beliefs with Unitarian Christian ideas, and addressed malpractices.
Priest at a Kali temple who became Narendranath's teacher.
Narendranath Datta, the most prominent symbol of Neo-Vedanta.
Freedom fighter turned philosopher: Integral Yoga.
Took both Neo-Vedanta and Vaishnava Vedanta along.
His philosophy is in the same Neo-Vedanta stream.
Composed the Satyarth Prakash and founded the Arya Samaj. It stresses logic, rejects caste and backs gender equality. He speaks of the Vedas, yet many of his beliefs stand close to Neo-Vedanta.
Neo-Vedanta's main work: treating the world as real and worth acting in, against the view that the world is mithya and freedom an illusion.
Poet-philosopher just before independence. His philosophy is universalistic and falls outside Neo-Vedanta and Hinduism, yet the speaker counts it as important.
Found that caste endured, converted to Buddhism in 1956, and wrote The Buddha and His Dhamma. He rejected traditional karma and Nirvana to create Navayana.
Ambedkar's new form of Buddhist philosophy, begun in 1956 in the 20th century.
Rejected all old beliefs and offered a new philosophy, popular especially in South India.
Formidable arguer who introduced dynamic meditation: meditation while dancing.
Learned women appear in the Upanishadic period, then participation almost vanishes. The speaker links it to low participation of women everywhere.

Born a Shakya prince at Kapilavastu. Tradition dates him about 563–483 BCE, though many scholars place him later. He left home at about 29, awoke at 35, taught for some 45 years and died at 80. The speaker says he was less a philosopher than a reformer who wanted society to stop suffering.

Two accounts. In the Buddhacharita, the four sights led him to leave one night on his horse Kanthaka with the charioteer Channa, who turned back at the Anoma river. In Ambedkar's account he left in place of a war: the whole community walked with him to the river and he asked them to go home and stop the fighting.

nodes.l: Sujata's kheer and the Middle Path
nodes.d: After six years of severe penance a woman named Sujata offered him a bowl of rice milk. He ate, bathed in the river and saw that the body must stay healthy to seek truth. His five companions, thinking he had fallen away, left him. The meal marked the turn to the Middle Path.
Questions the Buddha would not answer, because they do not help end suffering. Not ignorance but a crisis of expression.
Four-cornered logic: is it, is it not, both, neither. Each question about the world, soul or Tathagata was answered by none of the four.
Treat the wounded first, not the theory. Human civilisation is wounded; the task is relief.
Equal arguments for and against mean a question cannot be proven; mystical experience cannot be put into ordinary language.
18th-century German philosopher the speaker cites for a similar view that some questions cannot be settled by reason.
Sarvam Dukkham (suffering), its cause in ignorance, its cessation (Nirvana), and the path to it. Framed like a doctor's diagnosis.
Even what we call happiness is suffering: striving for it, guarding it, and losing it.
Ashtangika Marga: the eight-limbed path to end suffering.
The end of suffering (Dukkha Nirodha).
No fixed soul; consciousness is a continuous stream, like a flame that passes on. It explains rebirth.

One of the early schools after the Buddha, keeper of the Pali canon, which was first written down in Sri Lanka. The lecture uses 'Hinayana' and 'Theravada' together; 'Hinayana' (small vehicle) is the Mahayana's name for the early schools, not their own.
Grew from the Mahasanghika line; it considers Moksha as supreme bliss and accepts transfer of merit (Parinamana).
Later school within Mahayana, alongside Tantrayana and Mantrayana.
His last words: be your own light.
Whatever you do will return to you. Two rules: what you did cannot be destroyed, and what you did not do cannot reach you. Karma cannot be transferred.
Sanchita (accumulated), Prarabdha (now bearing fruit) and Kriyamana (being done now).
A conscious, immortal, eternal element in the body. Needed so that the person who acts is the person who reaps. Only Charvaka and Buddhism deny it.
Almost every Indian school except Charvaka holds it. It explains birth into poverty or wealth, and even justified caste, which some criticise.
All but Charvaka agree. Suffering comes in three kinds: supernatural, environmental and bodily.
Liberation from the cycle of karma and rebirth. It is permanent. In Semitic religions the goal is Heaven rather than liberation.
The root of bondage: we take ourselves to be the body.
Liberation comes through knowledge, though some add devotion or action.
The valid source of knowledge: every claim must name its evidence.
Plato, Socrates and Giordano Bruno spoke of it; Ian Stevenson studied claims of past lives for 40 years. Abrahamic faiths mostly reject it, though Sufis and the Jewish 'Gilgul' touch it.
The branch about values. It has two parts: ethics and aesthetics.
What is moral and what is not; whether moral rules should bend over time (is lying to save someone a sin?); what the purpose of life is; and what is good in itself, not merely as a means.

The study of beauty. Is beauty in the eye of the beholder (subjectivism), in the thing itself (objectivism), or shaped by culture? The speaker adds that even the beholder's eye is largely made by culture.
The third question of metaphysics: what are mind, intelligence and consciousness, and is there a soul beyond the body? Psychology began as part of philosophy.
The old claim that the world is made of atoms, made in India by Nyaya and in Greece by Leucippus and Democritus, long before science. Their atom differs from the one science later proved.
17th-century philosopher: 'I think, therefore I am'. The body does not think, so something else does, and that is the soul.
Computers reason, remember and now write stories without any soul, which puts pressure on the idea that thinking needs a soul and gives the Charvaka view a new hearing.
Kant's view: we cannot know about God or the soul. So believe if you wish, and do not trouble others for believing or not.
Seeing is not proof: the light, the senses or the mind's categories may each distort what we perceive (a fat dog taken for a small cow). Strong emotion or chemicals cause hallucinations.
Science assumes every event has a cause. Nyaya and Buddhist thinkers examined this; Hume called it an inductive habit, like concluding all pigeons are black after seeing a hundred.
Western philosopher who questioned the law of cause and effect as only an inductive argument.

Philosophy and science grew fastest where meditation, open discussion and freedom to think existed, even if not for everyone. The speaker places Indian philosophy at about 4,000 years and the Greek tradition from about 600 BC.
The speaker's own conclusion after studying philosophy: you learn that nobody knows the answers, and that you know as much as anyone does. A book distils decades of someone's thought into a few days.
Philosophy is applied to every field: of history, science, religion, politics. Each asks the deepest questions about how that field works.
Upanishadic statements such as Aham Brahmasmi, Tat tvam asi and Ayam Atma Brahma: the self (Atman) is Brahman.
Knowing one's original nature. In Indian philosophy it is knowledge of the soul or of what I am and am not. Mahavira, the Buddha, Shankara and Nanak are cited as examples.

nodes.l: Mysticism and the limit of language
nodes.d: Ordinary words come from ordinary shared experience, so a mystical experience has none. 'Mysticism' comes from muo, to be silent. Kabir's dumb man tasting jaggery and Rahim's verse make the same point.

In a dream we do not know it is a dream until we wake. Nagarjuna, the Buddhist brothers Asanga and Vasubandhu, and Shankara asked whether this practical world is a dream too. The speaker says it is a logical possibility, unproven, so we live as if life is real.
Buddhist philosopher brothers, grouped with Nagarjuna and Shankara for their similar views on the dream-like practical world.
For the common person, easy answers to hard questions and an organisation of beliefs. It offers peace, such as the soul being immortal so death only changes clothes.

From adhi + atma: connecting with something greater than oneself, whether God, Nirvana, Kaivalya, knowledge, or a feeling of unity with the whole world (extrovert mysticism). One can be spiritual without religion.

In the 6th century BCE iron tools spread across the Ganga plain. More land was ploughed and yields rose, giving farmers a surplus. Towns, markets and coined money followed. The speaker's rule: a philosopher says what his circumstances call for, so the Buddha cannot be understood without this world.

Small tribal territories merged into larger states, mostly monarchies and a few republics (gana-sanghas). Magadha (Rajgir), Kosala (Shravasti), the Vajji-Licchavi republic (Vaishali) and the Mallas (Kushinagar) frame the Buddha's whole life. Taxes paid for armies and wars; Kapilavastu of the Shakyas survived as a protected state of Kosala.

Kshatriyas and Vaishyas gained power and wealth but little standing in the Brahmin-led ritual order. Both Jainism and Buddhism came from Kshatriya founders and drew strong merchant support. The speaker reads this as a search for religious respect to match economic weight; it is one historians' interpretation, not proof of motive.

Around the 6th century BCE new ways of thinking appeared independently in several lands: the Shramanas in India, Confucius and Lao Tzu in China, Pythagoras and Heraclitus in Greece, Zoroaster in Persia. The term is Karl Jaspers'. The speaker uses it to place the Buddha among his contemporaries.
Greek thinker (about 500 BCE) who held that everything flows and no one steps into the same river twice. The speaker sets his impermanence beside the Buddha's; no link between them is known.
Greek mathematician and philosopher who also taught rebirth, which shows the idea was not only Indian.

Wandering ascetic teachers who challenged the Vedic ritual order and caste hierarchy. Buddhist texts speak of sixty-two views; seven teachers were famous and the Buddha was one. Six ran alongside him: Mahavira, Makkhali Gosala, Ajita Kesakambali, Purana Kassapa, Pakudha Kaccayana and Sanjaya Belatthiputta.

Compassion was one reason for the new stress on non-violence. Another was economic: ploughing needed cattle, and costly animal sacrifices drained farmers. Jains avoided farming because it harms living things in the soil and moved into trade, which helps explain their later prosperity.

Walked with Mahavira for about six years, then split from him. He founded the Ajivikas and taught that everything is fixed in advance. The speaker notes that his determinism is about 2,000 years older than Spinoza's.
Fatalist ascetic sect that rose with Makkhali Gosala. It held that outcomes are fixed whatever one does. It later faded from history.

Everything is destined, so deeds do not change the outcome. The speaker says people drift to it after disappointment, such as failing an exam after hard work. It conflicts with karma: if results follow actions, they cannot also be fated.

Taught agnosticism and scepticism: he would not say yes or no on rebirth, karma or the afterlife, since no one really knows. Sariputta and Moggallana were his best pupils before they went over to the Buddha. The speaker pairs him with Kant and Pyrrho in the West.
Taught that actions carry no moral consequence. The Buddha strongly opposed this, since denying karma risked spreading immorality.

Taught seven eternal elements: earth, water, fire, air, pleasure, pain and life. Since they only combine and separate, a sword passing through a body kills no one. The lecture runs him together with Ajita; the early texts list them as separate teachers.

The Jain view that reality has many sides, so every claim is partial. The speaker links it to the habit of saying 'I may be wrong' and to the Jain festival of forgiveness, when people ask pardon for the year's wrongs.

Part 1 is the Buddha's life. Part 2 is his own philosophy; Part 3 the Hinayana schools; Part 4 the Mahayana, with Shunyavada, Vijnanavada and Vajrayana; Part 5 the Navayana. After Buddhism the speaker plans the Vedic texts and the Gita, Shankara and Vaishnava Vedanta, the other Darshans, Western philosophy, philosophy of religion, and questions of equality and justice.

Vinaya Pitaka (monastic rules), Sutta Pitaka (the discourses) and Abhidhamma Pitaka (the deep philosophy, traditionally finished under Ashoka around 250 BCE). The Sutta Pitaka has five collections, including the Digha Nikaya, with the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, and the Khuddaka Nikaya, with the Jatakas, Dhammapada and Therigatha.

Called by King Ajatashatru of Magadha right after the Buddha's death, because his words might otherwise scatter. Upali, a barber by birth, recited the Vinaya; Ananda recited the discourses. Nothing was written; everything was memorised and chanted.
The texts stayed oral until they were written on palm leaves in Sri Lanka about 29 BCE, some 450 years after the Buddha's death. The long oral gap is one reason the life story has layers.

About 547 stories of the Buddha's earlier births, collected in the Khuddaka Nikaya. They are moral folklore: good evidence for what people believed, weak evidence for his life. The Kunala Jataka mentions the Rohini river quarrel.

Verses by about seventy-three early Buddhist nuns telling how they left home and walked the path. The speaker counts it among the most moving books in world literature and as proof that women had a real voice in the early community.

Poet-philosopher of the 1st–2nd century CE, linked to the Kushan king Kanishka and to the Mahayana. His Buddhacharita is the great Sanskrit life of the Buddha, which the speaker ranks with Kalidasa's work.

Ashvaghosha's Sanskrit poem in 28 cantos, of which only the first half survives in Sanskrit; the rest returns through Tibetan and Chinese translations. It gave the popular story of the four sights, with gods steering events, and reads the life through Mahayana eyes about five centuries after the Buddha.
A Mahayana sutra that tells the life with the most miracles: the Buddha descends from Tushita heaven, is born painlessly and takes seven steps. Historians read it as devotion built up over centuries.

Early Pali texts are sparse; Ashvaghosha dramatises the life; the Lalitavistara adds miracles; Ambedkar rewrites it on rational lines. The speaker's method is to tell both the traditional story and the Navayana one, and to say plainly which parts rest on thin evidence.

Ambedkar's book, finished in 1956 and published in 1957 after his death, meant as a Buddhist guide for India. It strips out the supernatural, rewrites the life, and drops traditional karma and rebirth. Traditional Buddhists objected that it should be called Ambedkar's Dhamma.

He doubted that a man of 28–29 had never seen age, illness or death; that a scientific mind would call all existence suffering; that a teacher of no-soul would also hold rebirth and Nirvana; and that a monks' order outside productive social life could be useful. His new account rests on these doubts.

In Ambedkar's account the Shakyas and Koliyas quarrelled over the Rohini river. The Shakya council voted for war and conscription; Siddhartha opposed it and faced exile, execution or his family's disgrace, and chose to leave as a monk so the war could be averted. The speaker finds the evidence thin: it rests on a Marathi biography, a Jataka and Kosambi, and the Jataka puts the dispute after his renunciation.
Maharashtrian social reformer and teacher who gave the young Ambedkar, after his school success, his Marathi life of the Buddha (published 1898). It already carried the Rohini story.

Scholar of Pali Buddhism whose Marathi Bhagavan Buddha (1940) and play Bodhisattva (1949) carry the Rohini theme. He was the father of the Marxist historian D. D. Kosambi, whom the lecture's wording blurs with him.

Queen Maya, travelling to her parents' home, gave birth in the Lumbini grove, now in Nepal. His mother died a week later and her sister Mahapajapati raised him. His father was Suddhodana of the Shakya clan at Kapilavastu. Miracles such as the seven steps come from later books.

Court dream-readers and the sage Asita foretold that the child would be a universal emperor or a great renouncer who becomes a Buddha. Asita wept because he would not live to see it. Suddhodana, fearing the second outcome, tried to make renunciation impossible.

He studied the Vedas and grammar, learned meditation and trained as a warrior, excelling at all. Gentle by nature, he shunned the hunt. When a bird he sheltered was claimed by his cousin Devadatta, who had shot it, the council ruled for the one who saved it, and the rivalry began.

His father arranged a marriage with Yashodhara, who chose him in a contest of skills over rival suitors. Accounts differ on ages; the lecture gives 20 and 16. Their son Rahula came years later. Suddhodana added seasonal palaces and a court of dancers to bind him to home.

In the Buddhacharita, outings showed him an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering mendicant, each arranged by the gods. He decided that day to renounce. Ambedkar doubted that a man of 29 had never seen old age, sickness or death.

After leaving, he went to Rajgir. Alara Kalama and then Uddaka Ramaputta taught him successively higher meditative states. He mastered them in days but saw the peace was personal and temporary, so the world's suffering was untouched. The lecture links them with Samkhya-Yoga and its three kinds of suffering; the early texts describe only the meditation levels.

King of Magadha at Rajgir. He offered the young seeker half his kingdom or a life of ease; the Buddha refused but promised to return. He later became a lay follower and gave the Veluvana garden to the monks. His son Ajatashatru starved him to death.

At Uruvela, by the Niranjana river, with five companions (Kondanna, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahanama and Assaji), he ate a bowl of rice and then a grain a day, wore rags and slept in cemeteries. After six years he saw that a starving body could not know anything and gave the path up.

After Sujata's meal he sat facing east under the pipal tree at Gaya, vowing not to rise without knowledge. At 35 he found answers to his two questions: why is there suffering, and how does it end. The lecture speaks of weeks of sitting; the early texts speak of one night's awakening.

He hesitated for seven weeks over whether to teach. People rely on God, a soul and heaven, and his truth offered none, so he feared no one would grasp it. A god (Brahma) is said to have asked him to teach for the world's sake, and he agreed.

He walked to Sarnath and found his five former companions. Their anger melted as he came near; they washed his feet and heard the Four Noble Truths. They took refuge, saying this was a teaching with no prophet, no single scripture and no miracle. This turning of the wheel of Dhamma began the community.

Yasa, a rich Varanasi youth sickened by a life of luxury, was won over within minutes. His parents and wife became the first lay followers and four friends became monks. With sixty monks trained, the Buddha sent them out to teach for the good of many.

Three matted-haired fire-worshipping brothers, Uruvela, Nadi and Gaya Kassapa, led about a thousand disciples. The Buddha won the proudest, Uruvela, by patient argument (the texts add legends of a fire-breathing serpent). They threw their sacrificial vessels into the river and joined him. At Rajgir, Bimbisara and a vast crowd followed.

Childhood friends and pupils of Sanjaya, seeking a better teacher. Assaji, one of the five, explained the Dhamma to Sariputta, and both joined the Buddha with 250 followers. Sariputta, the 'commander of the Dhamma', was famed for reasoning. They died before the Buddha, Sariputta in his native village and Moggallana at the hands of enemies.

Sudatta, a Shravasti banker known for feeding orphans. After a short talk he asked whether he must leave his wealth and work to become a monk; the Buddha said no. He bought Prince Jeta's garden by covering it with gold coins and built the Jetavana monastery.

The garden at Shravasti given by Prince Jeta and Anathapindika. The Buddha is said to have spent about nineteen rainy seasons there; the rains retreat is when monks stay in one place for four months. King Prasenajit of Kosala became a devotee but did not take robes.
King of Kosala at Shravasti and overlord of the Shakyas. He respected the Buddha, talked with him at length, and asked his help over the robber Angulimala. His son Jeta gave the Jetavana garden.

Head of the Shakya clan at Kapilavastu and the Buddha's father. The lecture shows him as a clan leader bound by the council rather than an absolute king. He feared the prophecy of renunciation, worked to keep his son at home, and died after the Buddha's return.

Wife of Siddhartha and mother of Rahula. Her anger at his leaving unannounced, and her later dignity, are retold by Maithili Sharan Gupta and, in a new way, by Ambedkar, who has her approve his going. She became the nun Bhadda Kaccana and, in his account, died the year he did.

Maya's sister (the lecture calls her the elder; the texts usually say younger), Suddhodana's second wife and the Buddha's foster mother. She led five hundred women to demand ordination and became the first nun.
The Buddha's only son, born about eight years after the marriage. On the Kapilavastu visit he asked his father for his inheritance and received the Dhamma, entering the community as a boy.

Cousin, son of Amitodana, and the Buddha's long-time attendant. He pleaded for the nuns, stood by the Buddha at his death and recited the discourses at the First Council. The lecture calls him the person closest to the Buddha.

Messengers sent by Suddhodana joined the Buddha and forgot to return, until Kaludayi persuaded him. The Buddha stayed in the Nigrodha garden and begged in his father's city; his father protested, and he answered that begging was the custom of his own lineage, the line of Buddhas. Yashodhara waited in her room; he went to her and she wept at his feet. Young Rahula asked for his inheritance and was given the Dhamma.

Court barber who shaved the heads of the Shakya princes (Ananda, Anuruddha, Bhaddiya and others) when they renounced. They asked the Buddha to ordain him first so that he would outrank them. He became the master of the Vinaya and recited it at the First Council.

After Suddhodana died, Mahapajapati Gotami and some five hundred Shakya women shaved their heads and walked to Vaishali. The Buddha refused three times, fearing practical dangers: angry families, quarrels, attacks. Ananda argued that women could reach liberation and that history would judge him, and the Buddha agreed on conditions. Yashodhara joined as Bhadda Kaccana; Amrapali joined later.

A feared robber in Kosala who killed travellers and wore their fingers as a garland, aiming for a thousand. The Buddha walked on calmly; when told to stop, he answered that he had stopped and the robber had not. Angulimala gave up violence and became a monk. He was stoned when he begged, and the Buddha told him to bear it.

Cousin and rival from the wounded-bird story. After joining the community he gained little power. When the Buddha was about 72 he asked to lead the Sangha and was refused. He then plotted with Prince Ajatashatru to kill Bimbisara and the Buddha.

Prince who killed his father Bimbisara and became king of Magadha, conquered the Vajji republic and sought the courtesan Amrapali. Haunted by guilt, he met the Buddha with Jivaka's help. He called the First Council after the Buddha's death.
Famed physician of Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and the Buddha. Texts credit him with remarkable surgeries, though how far they are authentic is uncertain.

Ajatashatru starved his father Bimbisara and took the throne. Devadatta's trained assassins could not strike the Buddha; a rolled boulder hurt his foot; the elephant sent to trample him did not attack. Ajatashatru later felt remorse, and Jivaka brought him to the Buddha, who forgave him.

City courtesan (nagarvadhu) of Vaishali, a respected role that forbade marriage. She invited the Buddha to a meal before the Licchavi princes could and would not give way to them. She gave her mango grove to the Sangha and became a nun. Another story says Ajatashatru loved her and used the tie to take Vaishali.

Sariputta and Moggallana died, Moggallana killed by enemies. In Ambedkar's account Mahapajapati and Yashodhara, both about 78–80, came to say farewell and died soon after; other traditions say Yashodhara outlived him. She spoke only gratitude for having known such a husband.

On his last journey he looked back at Vaishali, then ate at the house of Chunda the smith in Pava a dish called sukara-maddava, which some read as pork and others as a mushroom. Ill but calm, he bathed in the Kukuttha river, walked on to Kushinagar and died there after teaching his last disciple, Subhadda. He told Ananda that Chunda was blameless.

nodes.l: Funeral and the eight relic shares
nodes.d: The Mallas gave the body a royal cremation after a week of preparation. Ajatashatru, the Licchavis, the Shakyas and others armed themselves to claim the relics. The Brahmin Drona asked how followers of a man of peace could fight over his ashes, and divided them into eight equal shares for stupas, keeping the urn.

Pratityasamutpada: everything arises from conditions and nothing arises without a cause. The speaker says the whole Buddhist philosophy can be summed up in this one theory, which he leaves for Part 2. It supplies the cause of suffering in the Second Truth.

nodes.l: Dhamma without prophet, book or miracle
nodes.d: What struck the five companions was a teaching with no god-given authority, no single scripture and no miracle: events follow natural causes. The speaker stresses that the Buddha refused to be a prophet, so followers must test the Dhamma by their own conscience.

The path between palace luxury and six years of near-starvation; his own life showed both extremes failing. The lecture ties it to Sujata's bowl and then to right livelihood: do not renounce all wealth and do not be ruled by it.

The Buddha told Anathapindika that riches are not evil; the harm comes when money rules the mind. Someone who earns well and uses wealth for society serves it better than a monk. The speaker compares this with Gandhi's trusteeship and links it to Right Livelihood in the Eightfold Path.

Sotapanna (stream-enterer, at most seven more births), Sakadagami (one more), Anagami (none) and Arhat, who is liberated while alive and does not return. The Jains use Arihant for a similar ideal. Anathapindika became a stream-enterer after a short talk.

nodes.l: The Sangha and the rains retreat
nodes.d: The community of monks and nuns, supported by lay followers who gave food and land. Its rules are in the Vinaya. Monks begged each morning and meditated; for four months of the rains they stayed in one place, which is how monasteries grew. Ambedkar asked what such a body did for society.

The community took in people of any birth: Upali the barber, Sunita the scavenger, Sopaka and Suppiya who worked at the cremation ground, and the nun Prakriti of Chandala birth. Ananda used this record when he pleaded for women's entry.

Conditions for the nuns, such as that a nun, however senior, ranks below any monk and may not rebuke one. The speaker sees them partly as a practical bargain in a world hostile to women's orders; critics call them bias. He also notes the remark, probably later, that women's entry would halve the Dhamma's life.

Ananda asked who would lead. The Buddha named no one: the Dhamma would guide and the Sangha would decide together. The Pali texts say Mahavira's community quarrelled after his death. The Buddha left no ruler, no prophet's role and no sacred book; his last advice was to be a lamp unto oneself.

nodes.l: 'If you meet the Buddha, kill him'
nodes.d: A Zen saying (the transcript says Jainism, which looks like a mis-hearing) that the seeker should not lean on statues, books or even the teacher. The speaker's story of the monk who would call a plumber for a flushed scripture and sweep up a broken statue makes the same point: the Dhamma matters, not its objects.

In the Mahayana, a being bound for Buddhahood over many lives, passing ten stages. Stories of the Buddha's descent from Tushita heaven belong to this later view; the early texts do not have them. The speaker traces the Mahayana to the Mahasanghika split about a century after the Buddha; the full Mahayana took shape later.

Early school whose name means 'everything exists'. The speaker announces it for Part 3 with two branches, which I read as Vaibhashika and Sautrantika because the transcript garbles the names. Not yet taught in this lecture.
Mahayana school of emptiness, founded by Nagarjuna. Announced for Part 4; not yet taught in this lecture.
